Links: [{"title":"NASA’s Parker Solar Probe Captures 3I/ATLAS","url":"https://www.sci.news/space/nasas-parker-solar-probe-3i-atlas-14439.html"},{"title":"Parker Solar Probe / WISPR sees interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS","url":"https://wispr.nrl.navy.mil/node/78"},{"title":"Parker Solar Probe / WISPR sees interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS","url":"https://wispr.nrl.navy.mil/wispr-3I-ATLAS"},{"title":"Suggested Searches","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/?p=1186741"},{"title":"Parker 3I-ATLAS initial processing_thumbnail","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/?p=1187023"},{"title":"Astronomie - NASA’s Parker Solar Probe Observes Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS","url":"https://www.hjkc.de/_blog/26536-astronomie-nasa-s-parker-solar-probe-observes-interstellar-comet-3i-atlas/"},{"title":"Parker 3I-ATLAS initial processing_thumbnail","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/image-detail/amf-6c171fb6-ad2b-4d76-87b6-a2447f75e739/"},{"title":"Parker Solar Probe 3I/ATLAS initial processing","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/video-detail/amf-1af242b1-8b25-41c5-af4e-5c36790eb2b8"},{"title":"Parker Solar Probe 3I/ATLAS initial processing","url":"https://science.nasa.gov/?p=1186748"}]

NASA's Parker Solar Probe imaged the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in late 2025, and the results are preliminary.

- **Observation window:** The WISPR imager caught the comet between October 18 and November 5, 2025, a stretch when Earth-based telescopes could not see it because it sat in the Sun's glare. The probe took roughly ten frames a day.
- **Processing status:** NASA's initial images strip out the bright solar corona, but they still need final calibration. The NRL team released the raw data along with a rough processed version and noted that WISPR data normally waits about three months before release for that calibration.
- **Pointing:** The spacecraft had to roll along its axis to get the comet into view, which placed north at the bottom of the frames.
- **Other missions:** NASA says PUNCH, STEREO, and SOHO also observed the comet.

Sources: NASA's science site ([science.nasa.gov/image-detail/amf-6c171fb6-ad2b-4d76-87b6-a2447f75e739/](https://science.nasa.gov/image-detail/amf-6c171fb6-ad2b-4d76-87b6-a2447f75e739/)), the NRL WISPR page ([wispr.nrl.navy.mil/wispr-3I-ATLAS](https://wispr.nrl.navy.mil/wispr-3I-ATLAS)), and Sci.News ([sci.news/space/nasas-parker-solar-probe-3i-atlas-14439.html](https://www.sci.news/space/nasas-parker-solar-probe-3i-atlas-14439.html)).

The search turned up no 2026 paper reporting actual Psyche, Lucy, or Hera tail measurements. What it did find:

- **Psyche observations:** NASA reports that Psyche imaged 3I/ATLAS over eight hours on Sept. 8–9, 2025, when the comet was about 53 million km away, and that the images help refine its trajectory NASA's Psyche observed interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS over the course of eight hours on Sept. 8 and 9, when the comet was about 33 million miles (53 million kilometers) from the spacecraft.
- **Lucy observations:** Lucy's L'LORRI imager took a series of photos from Sept. 15–17, 2025, while the comet was heading toward Mars (Lucy's high-resolution, black-and-white imager, L'LORRI, captured a series of photos between Sept. 15–17, as the comet was zooming toward Mars.).
- **Campaign overview (2026 conference abstract):** An EPSC 2026 abstract by Eubanks et al. says at least 25 spacecraft observed the comet, and lists Psyche's Sept. 8 and Oct. 29, 2025 observations along with Lucy's Sept. 15–17 window (with at least 25 spacecraft observing 3I/ATLAS during its passage through the solar system.). This is a talk abstract, not a full paper.
- **Hera and tail immersion (predictions):** Grant and Jones (arXiv:2510.13222, to be published in RNAAS) predicted that spacecraft Hera will possibly be immersed within the ion tail of 3I/ATLAS during the period 25 October - 1 November 2025. This is a prediction. I found no result confirming a crossing.
- **Psyche pre-encounter planning:** A separate paper (arXiv:2508.15768) planned coordinated Psyche, Lucy, and Hera phase-angle measurements of the coma dust, but it is a planning document rather than a results paper.

Gap: I did not find a 2026 peer-reviewed paper reporting Psyche, Lucy, or Hera tail data. A follow-up search on the EPSC 2026 abstract or RNAAS publications could fill that in.

**Title:** An Interstellar Target of Opportunity: Lessons Learned from the 3I/ATLAS Spacecraft Campaign

**Authors:** Thomas Marshall Eubanks, Adam Hibberd, W. Paul Blase, Robert G. Kennedy III, and Andreas Hein

**Venue and date:** Europlanet Science Congress 2026, The Hague, 6–11 September 2026 (EPSC2026-759, Vol. 19, 2026; the citation lists 7–11 Sep 2026). The page was updated 02 Jul 2026.

**Relevant content:** The abstract does not mention an ion tail, solar wind, plasma instruments (Europa Clipper PIMS/ECM, Juice RPWI/PEP, MAVEN), or in situ tail crossings. It covers the broader observing campaign:

- **Discovery:** 3I/ATLAS was discovered on July 1, 2025, with an incoming velocity at infinity of 57.9778 km/s.
- **Scale:** At least 25 spacecraft observed it. These were 11 interplanetary spacecraft, 8 solar probes and observatories, and 6 space telescopes.
- **X-ray:** The abstract says observations were made at "IR, visual, UV and X-ray wavelengths," but gives no X-ray-specific details or numbers.
- **Solar observatories:** PUNCH, STEREO, SOHO, and GOES-19 monitored the integrated visual brightness from Sep. 12 to Nov. 13, 2025, when Earth-based observation was difficult or impossible.
- **Spacecraft observation windows:**
  - Psyche: Sep. 8 and Oct. 29, 2025
  - Lucy: Sep. 15–17, 2025
  - Five spacecraft at or orbiting Mars: Sep. 27 to Oct. 7, 2025
  - Europa Clipper: November 2025
  - Juice: Nov. 2–25, 2025
  - Juno: observations continuing into March 2026

If you need the ion tail, solar wind, or plasma instrument results, you would need the full presentation or supplementary material, which requires conference registration to access.

The search turned up one EPSC2026 abstract on 3I/ATLAS, plus related plasma-tail papers that are not from the meeting.

**EPSC2026 abstract:** EPSC2026-628, by Thomas Greathouse and co-authors, is an oral presentation titled "Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS Surrounded: Observations from 3 sister instruments." It was scheduled for Wednesday, 9 September, in Room Earth (Tango 1), at the Europlanet Science Congress 2026 in The Hague, 7–11 September 2026 (Oral | Wednesday, 09 Sep, 09:48–10:00 (CEST)| Room Earth (Tango 1)). The abstract page is at meetingorganizer.copernicus.org/EPSC2026/EPSC2026-628.html. The page snippet does not include the abstract text, so I can't confirm its findings. It is about the comet's surrounding gas environment, not specifically the ion tail.

**Not relevant:** EPSC2026-775 covers a Martian dust-storm plasma event, not 3I/ATLAS.

**Related non-EPSC work on the ion tail:** A WHT/WEAVE-LIFU study by Ferellec, Opitom and colleagues reports ion detections in the anti-solar tail, and it was published in MNRAS. It concludes that the comet is N2-rich, with a lower-limit N2/CO ratio of about 0.023 (arXiv 2609.05393; MNRAS volume 551, 2026). A Europa Clipper feasibility study (ResearchGate) examines whether the spacecraft could cross the comet's ion tail and detect pick-up ions and draped magnetic fields. That study estimates the tail could exceed 7.5 au in length.

I ran only one search, so the EPSC coverage may be incomplete. Searching the EPSC2026 programme directly for other 3I/ATLAS sessions would be the next step.

**Title:** "Interstellar Object 3I/ATLAS Surrounded: Observations from 3 sister instruments"

**Authors:** Thomas Greathouse, Kurt Retherford, Tracy Becker, Philippa Molyneux, and Cesare Grava (Southwest Research Institute, with Becker and Retherford also at the University of Texas at San Antonio), along with the Europa-UVS, JUICE-UVS, and LRO-LAMP science teams. This is an EPSC2026 abstract (EPSC2026-628).

**Summary:** The abstract reports ultraviolet observations of interstellar object 3I/ATLAS made by three SwRI-heritage spectrographs: Europa UVS, JUICE UVS, and LRO LAMP. The page describes the observations as taking place from November to December 2025, but the listed dates are all in November except one LRO-LAMP observation on 25 November.

- **Europa-UVS** observed on 6 November 2025 at a solar phase angle of about 143° and a comet-spacecraft distance of 1.09 AU.
- **JUICE-UVS** made a simultaneous observation on 6 November at about 12° phase angle and 0.44 AU. Other JUICE-UVS observations were on 2, 3, 5, 12, 19, and 25 November.
- **LRO-LAMP** observed on 25 November at about 30° phase angle and 1.98 AU.

Initial results show extended emissions from hydrogen (Lyman alpha at 121.6 nm), neutral oxygen (130.4 nm), and carbon (156.1 nm and 165.7 nm). The authors state that further calibration is needed before they can provide upper limits or firmer detections.

**Requested numbers:** The page contains no figures for the ion tail, solar wind, plasma, hydrogen corona, or production rates. The only quantitative values are the observation dates, solar phase angles, distances, and emission wavelengths listed above. The figure caption also gives the year of the JUICE-UVS observations as 2026, which conflicts with the November 2025 dates in the text.

The search turned up several research-style sources on 3I/ATLAS's tail geometry, plus some lower-quality pieces that I'd treat cautiously.

**Research-style sources:**
- A pre-perihelion study reports that the earliest coma extension pointed near position angles of 280° to 285°, and that later observations placed the tail near 95° to 106°. The authors could not tell whether the tail tracks the antisolar or the negative-velocity direction more closely, though they lean slightly toward the latter. (arXiv 2510.18769 notes the earliest coma extension near position angles of 280° to 285°, while later observations place the tail at 95° to 106°.)
- That same study says a very faint antisolar tail was measured in Hubble imaging from July 21, while the sunward fan still dominated the optical view. (Hubble imaging recorded a very faint antisolar tail on July 21, when the sunward fan still dominated.)
- A later inbound gas and dust paper reports a sunward jet at about 278° ± 2° and an antisolar dust tail at about 106° ± 4°. It also cites a separate August 2025 study that measured the jet at a mean of 280.7 ± 0.2°. (A relatively stable sunward jet sits at about 278° ± 2° east of north, while the antisolar dust tail appears at 106° ± 4°. and Jet position angle measurements at 6000 km from the optocenter average 280.7 ± 0.2°.)
- A spacecraft-exploration paper, which is a theoretical analysis rather than an observational result, gives the physics of the ion tail: the solar wind is much faster than the comet, typically 400 km/s or more, so ion tails tend to align radially in the anti-Sun direction. It also estimates that Hera, Lucy, and Europa Clipper would pass near or through the plasma tail around late October 2025.

**Lower-quality sources:** Popular news and blog pieces describe a well-defined ion tail extending about 0.7 degrees in November imaging, and a Gemini image that showed a tight coma but no obvious tail. A Substack post claims the object's tail points toward the Sun. That claim is not supported by the scientific sources, and I'd disregard it.

**Caveat:** I did not find a dedicated, peer-reviewed measurement of the ion (plasma) tail's position angle specifically. The position-angle values above mostly refer to dust and jet features, so a follow-up search targeting ion-tail measurements, such as CN or CO+ imaging, would be needed to fill that gap.

I didn't find the specific 2026 paper by Lisse, Bodewits, or Dennerl. The results cover the November–December 2025 XRISM and XMM-Newton observations of 3I/ATLAS and the solar wind charge-exchange explanation for them.

- **Observations:** XRISM's soft X-ray imager picked up an extended glow about 400,000 km from the nucleus, and XMM-Newton confirmed it in a 20-hour observation on December 3, 2025 (The XRISM "Xtend" soft X-ray imager detected a distinct, extended X-ray glow radiating approximately 400,000 kilometers (5 arcminutes) from the nucleus. This detection was subsequently validated by ESA's XMM-Newton observatory, which observed the object for 20 hours on December 3, 2025.).
- **Mechanism:** The emission is attributed to charge exchange, in which highly charged solar wind ions capture electrons from neutral gas molecules released by the comet. Only the 4-10 and 4-11 span of that source is supported by my results; it also notes that this mechanism has been observed in dozens of comets in the solar system since the 1990s.
- **Spectra:** One source says oxygen and carbon ions play a major role, as expected, though this is a secondary news summary.

Caveats on sources: the results include a Substack essay and a Zenodo preprint titled "On The X-Ray Silence of 3I/ATLAS" that contradicts the detections, and it is not peer-reviewed. A USA Herald piece claims a "forensic analysis" reopened questions about the XMM image, but it offers no verifiable method and I would not rely on it. For the actual paper, I'd search arXiv or ADS with the author names and "3I/ATLAS X-ray" directly.

{
  "message": "## Literature on solar-wind conditions at 3I/ATLAS and in Nov–Dec 2025 (searched 2026-10-17)

**Bottom line:** No published source gives measured or modeled solar-wind values at 3I/ATLAS for late Nov–early Dec 2025. That window covers the XRISM run (Nov 26–28) and the XMM run (Dec 3).
- The only comet-specific values are for the perihelion period, and they are assumptions or model ranges:
  - Hsu, Deca et al. (WSA-ENLIL, 400–600 km/s).
  - Grant & Jones (assumed radial 200/450/900 km/s, and 460 km/s).
- I found no XMM-Newton 3I/ATLAS paper anywhere (arXiv, journals, ADS-indexed pages). The XRISM ATel gives no solar-wind values.
- I found no CCMC Runs-on-Request entry for 3I. CCMC/DONKI servers were unreachable from my sandbox, so this is unverified. The only Jan Deca link I found is the Hsu et al. RNAAS note.
- I found no published Europa Clipper, Hera, MAVEN, Juice or Mars-orbiter in-situ plasma result for 3I.
- Limits of the search: ADS (no token), AGU abstracts and CCMC were not directly searchable. The arXiv API sweep found about 120 3I/ATLAS papers; I screened the plasma, X-ray and spacecraft-related ones.

### (A) 3I/ATLAS solar-wind and plasma items

**1. Hsu, H.-W., Deca, J., Horányi, M., Kempf, S., Cochrane, C. J., Jia, X., Phillips, C. B. — "Detectability of Dust and Ion Tails of Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS by Europa Clipper," RNAAS 9(11), 313 (Nov 2025).** doi:10.3847/2515-5172/ae2120. RNAAS is editor-screened, not refereed.
- The paper says: "Based on the latest available Wang–Sheeley–Arge ENLIL simulation" (a 2025 Nov 3–4 run, footnoted to NOAA SWPC), "the IMF around the 3I perihelion is well-represented by the Parker spiral … with solar wind speeds ranging between 400 and 600 km s⁻¹."
- The dominant pickup ion is CO₂⁺. Travel time from comet to Clipper is about 5 days.
- Predicted CO₂⁺ energy peaks: ~1 and ~110 keV at 400 km/s; ~5 and ~190 keV at 600 km/s.
- Predicted detection (below 6 keV, PIMS): Nov 7–9 at 400 km/s; Nov 9–11 at 600 km/s.
- Context: perihelion 2025-10-29 11:47 UT at 1.36 au; Clipper at 2.2 au.
- No IMF magnitude or density is given, and the ion code is not named (E×B pickup drift). There is no CCMC acknowledgment.

**2. Grant, S. R. & Jones, G. H. — "Prospects for the Crossing of Comet 3I/ATLAS's Ion Tail," RNAAS (2025).** doi:10.3847/2515-5172/ae12e6; arXiv:2510.13222 (Oct 15, 2025). I read the full text.
- The Tailcatcher model assumes purely radial wind at 200, 450 and 900 km/s. The tail simulation for 2025-11-01 uses 460 km/s.
- Europa Clipper: minimum miss distance about 8.0×10⁶ km, Oct 30–Nov 6, 2025. Hera: about 8.2×10⁶ km, Oct 25–Nov 1.
- No measured solar-wind values.

**3. Eubanks, T. M. et al. — "3I/ATLAS (C/2025 N1): Direct Spacecraft Exploration…," arXiv:2508.15768 (Aug 2025, preprint).**
- Says the solar wind is "typically 400 km/s or more"; the comet's speed at perihelion is 68.33 km/s.
- Hera, Lucy and Europa Clipper pass near the plasma tail on about Oct 24, 26 and 28, 2025, roughly 1 au from the nucleus.
- Their follow-up EPSC2026-759 abstract (Sep 2026) counts at least 25 spacecraft observing 3I, with no plasma data.

**4. Ferellec, L., Opitom, C., Snodgrass, C. — "Ion abundances in the plasma tail of 3I/ATLAS show that it is N2-rich," MNRAS 551, stag1402 (2026), refereed.** doi:10.1093/mnras/stag1402; arXiv:2609.05393. I read the full text.
- WHT/WEAVE-LIFU on 2025-11-30 and 12-02, at r_h = 1.8 au and Δ = 1.9 au.
- Detected N₂⁺, CO⁺, CO₂⁺, H₂O⁺ and CH⁺. N₂/CO > 0.023±0.001; H₂O⁺/CO⁺ = 0.35±0.02; CO₂⁺/CO⁺ = 1.4±0.1; CO₂⁺/H₂O⁺ = 3.8±0.4.
- The ion tail lies "close to the expected anti-solar direction." No solar-wind values.

**5. XRISM ATel #17523 — Ishi, D., Kanemaru, Y. et al. (JAXA/NASA/ESA/SRON), posted 2025-12-03.** https://www.astronomerstelegram.org/?read=17523 (not refereed).
- Observation: 2025-11-26 23:20 to 11-28 20:38 UT, 60 ks DDT, 14 slews.
- Possible extended emission of about 5′ radius in 0.3–1.0 keV.
- Background model: MWH kT 0.2 keV (EM 0.002 cm⁻⁶ pc), LHB 0.1 keV (EM 0.014), CXB Γ = 1.4 at 8.4 ph cm⁻² s⁻¹ keV⁻¹ sr⁻¹, a 0.525 keV O line, N_H = 1.77×10²⁰ cm⁻². Residuals near 0.4 and 0.6 keV.
- No comet flux, no distances, no solar-wind values.
- The JAXA release (https://www.xrism.jaxa.jp/en/topics/news/1208/) gives 17 h effective exposure, a glow of about 5′ (~400,000 km) and likely C, N, O excess. It notes cometary origin is not yet confirmed.

**6. XMM-Newton.** I found only press coverage (phys.org/ESA, Dec 2025): EPIC-pn, Dec 3, about 20 h, 282–285 million km from Earth. No flux and no solar-wind values. No paper found.

**7. CME forecasts at the comet (news only, not literature).**
- spaceweather.com, 2025-09-23: "a CME launched on Sept. 19th will reach Comet 3I/ATLAS on Sept. 24th or 25th," from "a NASA forecast model"; Watchers credits the image to NASA/ENLIL. No speed or density given; Eubanks pointed out the encounter.
- NextBigFuture (Nov 18, 2025): a CME "modelled as a direct hit on 3I/Atlas around November 22, ~12:00 UTC." No model or source is named, and I could not verify it.
- I found no credible report of a 3I tail-disconnection event. A Zenodo item claiming a Jan 9, 2026 disconnection is not credible.

**8. Spacecraft observations without plasma values.**
- Zhang & Battams, PASP 138, 014403 (2026), refereed: STEREO-A HI1/COR2, LASCO C3 and CCOR-1 photometry; brightness scales as r^(−7.5±1.0).
- Eubanks, DeForest et al., arXiv:2511.20810 (preprint): PUNCH and coronagraph tracking Oct 8–30. No ion-tail or solar-wind content.
- PSP/WISPR imaged Oct 18–Nov 5, 2025 (NRL/NASA pages). Data are uncalibrated and there is no paper.
- Juice: MAJIS paper arXiv:2607.08603 (preprint) gives Q(H₂O) of 8→4×10²⁸ s⁻¹ over Nov 2–25 at 1.36–1.68 au. A SETI piece (Jun 2026) says Janus saw "plasma interactions" changing the ion tail, preliminary and with no numbers.
- Europa Clipper UVS on Nov 6 at 164 million km. Whether PIMS or ECM saw tail signatures was "still underway" as of Jan 2026 (SETI).
- EPSC2026-628 (Greathouse et al.): Europa-UVS, JUICE-UVS and LRO-LAMP Ly-α/O/C, no plasma numbers.
- MAVEN IUVS (Sep 27–Oct 7): press only, D/H upper limit. No SWIA/STATIC/MAG results found.
- Tianwen-1 (Ren et al., ApJL, doi:10.3847/2041-8213/ae61b3): dust only.
- SOHO/SWAN water production: Combi et al., ApJL 998, L17 (2026) gives 3.17×10²⁹ s⁻¹ on Nov 6 at 1.40 au, falling to 1–2×10²⁸ by Dec 9. Tan et al., ApJL 998, L22 gives a peak of about 4×10²⁸. Neither quotes solar-wind charge-exchange rates.

### (B) Solar wind, Nov–Dec 2025

**9. Yasyukevich, Y. et al. — "The 12 November 2025 Ugly Duckling Geomagnetic Storm: From the Sun to the Earth," Sensors 26(5):1490 (Feb 27, 2026), refereed (MDPI).** doi:10.3390/s26051490. Uses ACE data at L1, time-shifted.
- **Shock-1:** 11 Nov ~22:15 UT, from the Nov 9 CME (X1.7). Speed ~400→500 km/s; B 5→12 nT.
- **Shock-2:** 11 Nov ~23:48 UT in the text, 23:38 in the table, from the Nov 10 CME (X1.2). Speed ~460→730 km/s; Bz to −54 nT.
- **ICME-2:** about 04:00–15:30 UT on Nov 12. Proton density 10–11 cm⁻³; plasma β ≈ 0.5.
- **Shock-3:** 12 Nov 18:53 UT, from the X5.1 CME (flare peak 10:04 UT Nov 11). Speed ~920 km/s; B ~20→38 nT; Bz about −14 nT.
- **ICME-3:** from about 04:00 UT on Nov 13.
- Indices: Dst −217 nT, SYM-H −254 nT, Kp 9−.
- Type II shock speeds: 804 km/s (Nov 9), 1320 km/s (Nov 10), 1350 km/s (Nov 11).
- **Flag:** the paper is internally inconsistent on the Shock-2 time, on Kp (8.667 vs 9−), and on the AR location. Dynamic pressure appears only in a figure.

**10. Corroborating operational and other sources for Nov 11–12.**
- SWPC daily report (RSGA) for 11-2100Z to 12-2100Z: peak 969 km/s at 12/1946Z; total IMF 61 nT at 12/0036Z; Bz −55 nT at 11/2357Z.
- ESA (Nov 21, 2025): CME ~1500 km/s, arrival 18:50 UTC Nov 12.
- CCMC CME Scoreboard: 1856 km/s, half-angle 45°; L1 arrival ~18:52Z with B rising from 19 to ~40 nT. From search snippets; not opened.
- Other Nov 12–13 papers:
  - Xiong et al., arXiv:2603.14454 (preprint): Dst −214 nT; gives no solar-wind values in the abstract.
  - Picanço et al., Space Weather (2026), doi:10.1029/2026SW005063, refereed: not read.
  - GLE77 preprints: arXiv:2601.22807 and arXiv:2601.19289.

**11. Late Nov–early Dec 2025 at L1 (operational only; I found no paper).**

SWPC RSGA values, verified on spaceweatherlive.com:

| Window (UTC) | Peak speed | Total IMF | Max southward Bz |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25/2100–26/2100 Nov | 838 km/s at 26/0924Z | 8 nT | −6 nT |
| 26/2100–27/2100 Nov | 779 km/s at 26/2242Z | 7 nT | −6 nT |
| 27/2100–28/2100 Nov | 707 km/s at 27/2158Z | 7 nT | −5 nT |
| 01/2100–02/2100 Dec | 465 km/s | 7 nT | −4 nT |
| 02/2100–03/2100 Dec | 530 km/s | 17 nT at 03/2055Z | −13 nT |
| 03/2100–04/2100 Dec | 771 km/s at 04/1112Z | 22 nT at 03/2231Z | −13 nT at 04/0226Z |

- The Nov 25–30 stream was a coronal-hole high-speed stream: about 700–820 km/s on Nov 25–27, decaying to about 600 by Nov 30 (EarthSky daily logs, which give no densities).
- An X1.9 flare occurred at 01/0249 UTC Dec 1 (SWPC). It produced a partial-halo CME, type II ~988 km/s (Watchers), mostly non-Earth-directed.
- Dec 3–4: a CIR plus recurrent negative-polarity coronal-hole stream, with a possible glancing blow from the Dec 1 CME (SWPC forecast discussion). G3 was reached at 18–21 UT on Dec 3 (Australian forecast centre Warning 25/96).
- Dec 6: M8.1 full-halo CME (20:39 UT, type II ~1143 km/s). SWPC issued a G3 watch for Dec 9, but the storm did not materialize.
- I found no STEREO-A in-situ analysis, no heavy-ion or charge-state values (ACE SWICS) and no paper on the Nov 28–Dec 4 interval.

**Caution:** all of item 11 is near-Earth L1 data, not at the comet. Values at the comet need a longitude/radial mapping, which no published source has done for 3I.
